recent_posts.title: Seeing MCP
recent_posts.summary: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is expanding rapidly across enterprises, creating a new wave of API sprawl similar to previous REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and Kafka expansions — but faster and wider. The challenge of 'seeing' and governing these APIs remains largely unsolved, and the common assumption that AI will handle discovery and documentation automatically is questioned. Machine-readable artifacts combined with LLMs like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini offer some promise for automated discovery and visualization, but new blind spots will emerge. The author is building tooling to generate side-by-side documentation for APIs, MCP servers, and Agent Skills, advocating for ephemeral and evolving approaches to API visibility rather than static ones.

recent_posts.title: Wrestling With API Complexity
recent_posts.summary: A reflective personal essay on the appeal of wrestling with API complexity. The author draws parallels between exploring APIs and youthful adventures, describing the intellectual thrill of deep research, pattern recognition across many APIs, and sitting with uncertainty. The piece touches on how AI is adding new layers of complexity to the API landscape, and how most people are currently struggling to navigate it — financially motivated or otherwise.

recent_posts.title: Publishing Plans, Rate Limits, and FinOps for 3,837 API Providers
recent_posts.summary: A large-scale project to publish machine-readable API pricing, rate limit, and FinOps artifacts for 3,837 API providers in the API Evangelist GitHub network. Three new YAML artifact types were generated: API Commons Plans & Pricing, API Commons Rate Limits, and a FinOps Foundation FOCUS v1.3-aligned cost framework. Of these, 184 Tier 1 providers were manually reconciled with real vendor pricing data, including frontier AI labs, payment platforms, SaaS tools, and cloud providers. The motivation is to close the financial gap in API contracts — OpenAPI describes how to call an API but not what it costs, which is critical for AI agents making autonomous decisions across many providers. Key findings: AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are the most transparent; classic SaaS providers are mid-transparent; Fortune 500 enterprises almost universally hide pricing behind partner sales contacts. Next steps include wiring artifacts into APIs.json, publishing feeds at apis.io, and building CI-based reconciliation pipelines.

recent_posts.title: We Standardized the API. We Didn't Standardize the Application.
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of creating API applications across six major providers — Notion, Slack, LinkedIn, GitHub, Cloudflare, and Google — reveals that while OpenAPI standardized how to describe APIs, there is no standard for how to become a consumer of one. Each provider uses different vocabulary, gating mechanisms, scope models, and credential types. The divergence was tolerable when developers managed a handful of APIs, but becomes a serious problem as API counts scale and AI agents need to navigate these portals programmatically. Slack's JSON/YAML app manifest is highlighted as the only agent-friendly artifact among the six. The post argues for a cross-provider application manifest standard that captures credential types, scope vocabularies, resource selection models, verification states, and TTL/rotation policies.

recent_posts.title: Why API knowledge translates into organizational power and career growth
recent_posts.summary: Drawing on experience at the Department of Veterans Affairs and years of API consulting, the author argues that knowing where APIs are, who owns them, and how they work translates directly into organizational power and career advancement. By discovering, reverse engineering, documenting, and building relationships around APIs, professionals accumulate knowledge of the technical, business, and political systems that drive their organizations. This dynamic has existed since the mobile era and is intensifying with the rise of AI-powered applications.

recent_posts.title: Guardrails, Not Gates: Supreet Nagi on Taming the API Jungle
recent_posts.summary: A review and endorsement of Supreet Nagi's handbook 'From Chaos to Connectivity: The API Practitioner's Handbook', which reframes API governance from centralized review boards (gates) to automated, pipeline-integrated guardrails. The handbook proposes a four-workflow closed-loop model: Deployment (Policy-as-Code in CI/CD), Endorsement (tiered compliance scoring), Reporting (live governance dashboard), and Retirement (zombie API detection via telemetry). Central to the model is the 'Golden Path' — a pre-approved, compliant stack that makes the right way to ship also the easiest way. The handbook also argues that well-governed, machine-readable API catalogs are essential grounding infrastructure for AI agents operating against enterprise systems.

recent_posts.title: The Business and Politics of Platform Status Page Details
recent_posts.summary: GitHub recently updated its status page with a new 'degraded performance' state, per-service uptime metrics, and clearer communication around model availability. The author, who has tracked API status pages for over a decade, reflects on the evolution of platform status pages as a standard building block for API providers. While welcoming the transparency, the author raises questions about the business and political implications — particularly how introducing new states like 'degraded performance' might affect service level agreements and whether such transparency efforts ultimately serve platforms more than users.

recent_posts.title: That List of 1000 APIs Does Not Do Me Much Good When I Just Need To Be Capable of Doing Something
recent_posts.summary: A veteran API evangelist reflects on the futility of massive API directories and integration provider icon walls. After 16 years in the space, the author argues that API discovery needs to evolve beyond listing thousands of APIs toward capability-based vocabulary artifacts that meet users where they are. The post explores early experiments with a 'vocabulary' artifact for the Google Analytics API and suggests that agentic AI, combined with new discovery approaches, may offer a path forward — but isn't the complete answer.

recent_posts.title: An API Consumer Interoperability Mindset
recent_posts.summary: Most API tooling and discourse is built around an API producer mindset, but the real value lies in consuming APIs effectively. The author argues that thinking like an API consumer — understanding how APIs fit together across providers — is a rare and undervalued skill. Using MCP servers from Notion or Figma as examples, the point is made that producer-defined interfaces only go so far; true power comes when consumers define exactly what resources, functions, and context they need across multiple APIs. The rise of agentic workflows is shifting power away from individual API producers and toward a consumer-centric perspective that breaks down boundaries between services.

recent_posts.title: Questioning Our API Governance Reality
recent_posts.summary: A critical reflection on the current state of API governance, questioning whether design-rule linting (via Spectral/Vacuum applied to OpenAPI/AsyncAPI) can realistically standardize APIs across enterprise teams. The author demonstrates an alternative approach using the Naftiko framework to normalize inconsistent path and parameter conventions (camelCase, snake_case, PascalCase) from multiple upstream services into a single consistent interface. Key critiques include: governance focuses almost exclusively on APIs produced rather than consumed, lacks alignment with runtime policy tools (OPA, Cedar), ignores operational concerns like documentation and SDKs, and suffers from over-centralization. The author argues for domain- and industry-specific policy sets, team autonomy, and governance tied to business outcomes rather than uniform technical rules.

top_posts.title: OpenAPI Doctor is What API Innovation Looks Like Today
top_posts.summary: OpenAPI Doctor by Princess B33f Heavy Industries enhances API management by making OpenAPI and Spectral more visually manageable. The tool offers creative visual enhancements and abstracts complex rules to improve usability. It supports exploring API infrastructure with better visibility of requests and responses. Users are encouraged to try it out with their own OpenAPI specs and experience its functionalities, including YAML view and governance rule applications.

top_posts.title: Adopting MCP is a Bad Idea
top_posts.summary: The author argues against adopting MCP, citing several reasons ranging from business and political factors to technical complexities. They emphasize that MCP adds another layer of complexity without solving existing issues and serves the interests of those looking to access and exploit user data. The post advocates for alternative approaches like OpenAPI and JSON Schema for managing digital resources more effectively.

top_posts.title: Agents. It Is All APIs. Nothing Has Changed
top_posts.summary: AI agents are not a new concept but rather the latest rebranding of long-standing API and web automation work. The infrastructure for machine-readable data, hypermedia, semantic web standards, and automated agent interactions has existed for over a decade. What's being marketed as revolutionary "agentic" technology is actually established API economy practices being repackaged with new terminology by investors seeking the next financialization wave. The real work involves continuing to build machine-readable standards and APIs that serve both human and automated consumers, regardless of current hype cycles.

top_posts.title: Applying Domain-Driven Driven Design to Integration and Consumption
top_posts.summary: Explores applying domain-driven design principles to API consumption and integration, not just production. Discusses how concepts like bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, and aggregates help API consumers manage third-party services by establishing control over how multiple APIs work together, even when individual API designs are outside their control. Challenges the notion that DDD only applies to API producers.
